---
title: "Story"
---

My scientific work has developed around a recurring problem: how to describe molecular systems that are too large, heterogeneous and slowly evolving for conventional atomistic simulations, but too chemically specific to be treated as generic soft matter.

This problem has followed me through different systems and methods: polymers, coarse-grained models, reverse mapping, hybrid particle--field molecular dynamics, biomembranes, nanocomposites, polymer brushes, nanoplastics and software development.

## From molecular detail to larger scales

My early work was rooted in molecular simulation of polymeric and soft-matter materials. These systems are chemically rich, but their relevant behaviour often emerges at scales that are difficult to reach with atomistic molecular dynamics alone.

This led me to work on coarse-grained models and reverse-mapping strategies: ways of moving between molecular detail and simplified representations without losing the structural and chemical identity of the system.

## Particles and fields

A major step in this trajectory was the development and use of hybrid particle--field molecular dynamics. In this approach, molecular particles preserve architecture, connectivity and chemical identity, while density fields describe collective non-bonded interactions and mesoscale organization.

This particle--field viewpoint has shaped much of my work since then. It offers a way to extend molecular simulation toward larger and more complex systems, while keeping a direct connection to molecular chemistry.

## From methods to chemical soft matter

Over the years, I have applied and extended these ideas to a range of chemically complex soft-matter systems, including polymer melts, surfactants, biomembranes, polymer nanocomposites, carbon black--polymer interfaces, grafted polymers, brushes and micro/nanoplastics.

The common thread is not a single material class, but a methodological question: how can molecular simulation remain chemically meaningful when collective organization, interfaces and morphology become essential?

## OCCAM

The development of OCCAM is part of this same trajectory. OCCAM is a hybrid particle--field molecular dynamics platform designed to make chemically specific density-field simulations scalable and usable for large soft-matter systems.

For me, software is not separate from scientific vision. It is the place where ideas about models, approximations, algorithms and applications become testable.

## Where this leads

My current work continues this path. I am interested in density-based descriptions that remain connected to molecular chemistry and can help describe structure, organization and behaviour in complex soft matter.

The broader goal is to build molecular simulation approaches that are physically grounded, chemically meaningful and useful for systems where molecular detail and mesoscale organization cannot be separated.
